title: Hong Kong's IPO boom and the compliance functions scrambling to keep up
summary: Hong Kong's IPO market hit HK$388 billion in nine months, and the compliance implications are serious. Alex and Jordan dig into what a volume surge of this scale means for AML controls, overdue HKMA obligations, and what MLROs need to do before week's end.
script:
BLANK_LINE

ALEX: Here is the number that should be sitting in every Hong Kong compliance officer's head this morning. HK$388 billion raised in IPOs across the first nine months of 2026 alone. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po confirmed that figure yesterday, and it has already surpassed the full-year total for 2025. Jordan, I want to start there because I do not think the financial crime community has fully absorbed what that volume means for their controls.

JORDAN: They haven't. And I'll tell you why. When deal volumes double in under a year, the pressure lands first on the front line, on relationship managers, on customer due diligence teams, on the people doing KYC refresh for listing sponsors and their clients. It doesn't land on the risk framework because the risk framework was calibrated for a quieter market. So what you've got is a structural mismatch, and most compliance functions don't even know it yet.

ALEX: I'd push back slightly, because the HKMA has been reasonably clear in its guidance, particularly under paragraph eleven of the AML and CFT Guideline, that supervised institutions need to reassess their ML and TF risk exposure when business volumes shift materially. This isn't a gap in the supervisory framework. The expectation is already there. The question is whether firms are acting on it.

JORDAN: Right, and that's exactly the gap. The expectation is there in the text. The reality, from conversations I've had with people running AML functions at mid-tier institutions, is that nobody has gone back to the board to say our risk appetite statement was written for a market doing HK$200 billion a year, not HK$400 billion. That conversation isn't happening at the speed it needs to.

ALEX: And the timing matters here. The HKMA's annual AML and CFT self-assessment cycle for institutions closes at the end of this month. The self-assessment under paragraph eleven covers customer due diligence, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, STR filing quality, training, governance, and independent audit. If your institution's risk profile has materially changed because of IPO activity and you haven't updated the self-assessment to reflect that, you've got a problem that will be visible to the examiner.

JORDAN: That's the right frame. But I want to go one level more specific. The IPO pipeline creates specific typology risks that are easy to overlook in a self-assessment written at a high level. Nominee shareholders, complex pre-IPO restructuring, listings involving jurisdictions with elevated ML risk, short-term holding patterns after listing date. These are not theoretical. They're exactly the patterns FATF Recommendation twenty-four is designed to address when it comes to beneficial ownership of legal persons. If your self-assessment isn't touching those specifically in the context of your IPO-related business, it's too generic.

ALEX: So what should listeners do, practically, before the end of this week?

JORDAN: Three things. First, if you're the MLRO or head of AML at an institution that participates in the Hong Kong IPO market, either as a listing sponsor, a custodian, or a lender to pre-IPO investors, pull your most recent risk appetite statement and check whether it has any reference to elevated deal-volume scenarios. If it doesn't, that's a gap you need to document and escalate before the self-assessment closes. Second, brief your compliance committee or risk committee on the volume context. The HK$388 billion figure is the kind of number that changes what examiners ask when they walk in. You want your board and senior management to have seen it before an examiner cites it to them. Third, check your transaction monitoring calibration. Alert thresholds set twelve months ago were set for a different market. If you haven't done a scenario-review specifically for IPO-related flows since volumes surged, that's your priority for the week.

ALEX: Moving on to an obligation that is technically overdue and still live. The HKMA issued a thematic review of STR narrative quality in the fourth quarter of last year, and around twenty-five percent of authorised institutions received deficiency letters in early 2026. The closure of those findings is a current obligation. Jordan, I know you have a strong view on this one.

JORDAN: I do, because "STR narrative quality" sounds like a documentation issue and it isn't. It's a judgement issue. The feedback we're seeing consistently, and this is not unique to the HKMA thematic, is that STRs are being filed with adequate transaction data but inadequate reasoning. The JFIU needs to understand why the institution thought this was suspicious, not just what happened. If your STR reads like a transaction chronology with a conclusion bolted on the end, it won't meet the standard.

ALEX: And that's a training issue as well as a process issue. But I'd note that the HKMA has been patient here. The thematic findings were issued early in the year, and institutions have had months to respond. If you're one of the twenty-five percent who received a deficiency letter and you haven't closed those findings, the self-assessment return this month is not the moment to still have open items from a thematic review. That combination will attract attention.

JORDAN: Agreed. And for institutions in Singapore, a quick note: the MAS Notice 626 quarterly STR governance review, covering completeness, timeliness, escalation effectiveness, and reconciliation of STRO acknowledgements, was due in July. If that review hasn't been formally signed off and documented, do it now. The September quarter-end review is coming up and you want a clean record.

ALEX: One item worth flagging on the horizon before we close. Hong Kong's Chief Executive has signalled that legislation is coming to address disputes and crimes arising from artificial intelligence applications, with experts calling specifically for statutory frameworks covering data governance and algorithmic safety. This is early-stage, but the direction is clear. For compliance functions that are deploying AI in transaction monitoring, customer risk scoring, or name screening, the regulatory environment around those tools is going to get more structured. Now is the right time to document how those models work, who governs them, and what the human-review layer looks like.

JORDAN: And if that documentation doesn't exist yet, that's not a future problem. That's a current one. The question examiners in every jurisdiction are already asking is not whether you use AI. It's whether you can explain what it does and show that a person is accountable for its outputs.

ALEX: That's the one to carry into the week. The full obligation register and source links for everything we've discussed today are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. I'm Alex.

JORDAN: I'm Jordan. If any of that self-assessment conversation felt uncomfortably close to your current situation, act on it today rather than at the end of the month. See you tomorrow.
